title: Learning without the theatre
dek: Why my project write-ups admit what they have not verified, and what that admission costs.
body: Several of my project write-ups contain a line saying their dates still need verifying. The L3 page says outright that it needs a deeper commit-level pass and that the only window I have actually confirmed is April 11 to April 12, 2026. I left those lines in. They make the pages look unfinished, which is accurate.

The alternative is theatre: rewriting a hackathon weekend as a considered engineering programme. SkyPrint is the clearest case. Its first commit is April 18, 2026 at 3:08 PM, and the deterministic scoring work lands after 5 AM the following morning. It also carries the longest follow-up list of anything I have built, with no tests on the scoring logic, no methodology citations, and no error handling for missing aircraft or route data. I could call it a climate-tech platform and stop talking. The timestamps stay on the page because they are the honest explanation of why that list looks the way it does.

The other place theatre creeps in is team projects. Sprouted's README lists me as a team member, and my write-up states that as a plain fact before it says anything about what I did. EmptyNEU is a group repository too. Going back through those timelines, the verbs carry most of the weight. I built the seed data flow and the Docker boot change. I helped merge and combine other people's persona pages, and helped resolve the navigation conflicts that came with them. Helped is not a smaller word than built. It is a different word, and using built in its place would be a small lie a teammate could catch.

Both of those pages carry a follow-up item asking for exact per-teammate contribution references and PR links. I have not done it yet. Until I do, those sections rest on my own memory of who did what, which is the least reliable source available to me.

The part I find genuinely hard is that this is not free. A page admitting that exact commit dates should be verified reads as weaker than one that simply asserts them, and someone skimming may see only hedging. I have decided I would rather be checkable than impressive, but I want to be clear that it is a trade rather than a costless virtue. The version of me that wants a job is not always the version writing these pages.

What the trade buys is that I can read my own work a year later and believe it. I know which projects have tests and which only have a plan for tests. I know PyStruct does not report source locations in its error messages yet, because the page says so, not because I happen to remember. None of these write-ups are load-bearing on my good opinion of myself, which makes them much cheaper to keep updating.
